hints: Notice the change of state here, heating solid aluminium chloride gives a simple molecular vapour, so think about what that tells you about ionic versus covalent character.
Picture two $\text{AlCl}_3$ units joining together, each Al is electron deficient with only 6 electrons, while Cl has lone pairs to share.
Count how the bridges form, some Al-Cl links are normal shared pairs and the bridging links are formed when Cl donates both electrons, giving two bond types in one molecule.
walkthrough:
**Compare Solid And Vapour**

Solid aluminium chloride has a giant ionic lattice with $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. On heating it sublimes to form discrete $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ molecules, which must be covalent to exist as separate low melting molecules.

**Look At The Electron Deficiency**

A single $\text{AlCl}_3$ molecule has only 6 electrons around Al, so it is electron deficient. It dimerises to $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ so each Al can reach an octet.

Joining idea:
$$2\text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$$

**Spot The Two Types Of Covalent Bond**

In the dimer, each Al has two terminal Al-Cl bonds where one electron comes from each atom. That is normal covalent.

The two bridging Cl atoms each use a lone pair to form an extra link to the other Al, where both electrons come from Cl. That is coordinate (dative covalent).

So $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ contains covalent and coordinate bonding together.

options.A: Correct. The $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dimer is a covalent molecule with four terminal normal covalent Al-Cl bonds plus two bridging Cl atoms that form dative covalent bonds to complete the octet on Al.
options.B: Tempting but incomplete. It correctly rejects ionic bonding in the vapour, but it misses that the bridging Al-Cl-Al links are formed by Cl lone pair donation, which is specifically coordinate (dative covalent) bonding.
options.C: Incorrect. There is no ionic bonding in the discrete $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ molecule. Students sometimes choose this because solid $\text{AlCl}_3$ is ionic, but heating converts it to a covalent molecular form.
options.D: Incorrect. Ionic only describes the solid lattice $\text{Al}^{3+}$ with $\text{Cl}^-$, not the vapour dimer. $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ exists as separate molecules with shared electron pairs, so it cannot be ionic only.
